Tech sector breadth is rapidly improving:

75% of S&P 500 technology sector stocks finished above their 200-day moving average last week, the highest percentage since October 2024.

This marked the first time in 219 trading days that this threshold was reached, ending the 9th-longest streak on record.

By comparison, the longest stretch during which fewer than 75% of tech stocks traded above their 200-day moving average lasted 759 trading days, ending on April 22, 2003, following the Dot-Com Bubble burst.

Historically, each time such a streak ended, the technology sector returned +2.5% on average over the following month and +7.3% over the next 3 months.

After 6 months and 12 months, the average gains were +15.5% and +33.4%, respectively.

Meanwhile, 69% of Nasdaq 100 stocks are now trading above their 200-day moving average, near the highest percentage since July 2025.

The tech stock rally is gaining momentum.

In this conversation, a16z's Joe Schmidt, Andy McCall, and Elena Burger sit down to discuss the lighthouse and landgrab playbooks for selling enterprise AI: win marquee logos so proof travels, or win budgets that already exist.

"'100% of this text is AI' is the new Scarlet Letter of dunking on people and posts."

"I hate to give the French credit for anything, but the 1960s semantic thinkers who created 'French Theory' really cooked when they anticipated Pangram and AI authorship 80 years ago."

"There are certain tells that you can spot where, it's like, 'This is a coherent sentence, but there's no way a human wrote this.'"

"To bastardize Voltaire, if a wise and brilliant author doesn't exist, the LLM has to invent one."

"People want authorship. They want authorship because it is meaning, because the indexing and relation and handling of ideas is itself the meaning of the idea."

In other words, the US government now spends more money just on interest than it does to fund the entire US Military or to provide healthcare for seniors.

Today it prices a hike.

The entire easing trade got repriced to tightening in 7 months. 

Higher-for-longer stopped being a warning and became the base case. 

For now this is bad for long bonds.

I think Jane Street being LeBron is partly the point.

New technologies usually earn wildly different returns depending on who's using them, especially early on. The best operators figured out electricity, computers, the internet, etc. well before the average company did.

So, I wouldn't extrapolate Jane Street's hurdle rate to everyone. But it is a useful data point for what GPUs can earn in the hands of a firm that's excellent at turning compute into money.

And unlike a basketball, AI may eventually transfer some of LeBron's technique to the rest of us 🏀👍

This all gets tiring after a while.

"Macro Strategist" calls me out saying I have no idea what I'm talking about when it comes to rates, completely unprovoked.

I show him how his own view on rates was drawing a parallel channel in 2023 telling people rates were going to -2 to -3% in 2024/2025, so he should have some humility and drop the ego.

He then deletes his post calling me out, deletes his old bad prediction (I took the screenshot because I thought he might accidentally do that), then blocks me.

If you are going to promote yourself as a macro strategist, have the courage to publicly learn from your wrong calls (as I often get things wrong).

Don't go around mocking others, and especially not when your own views have been dead wrong.

The reason I have not been as active on X the last few months is because I get tried of dealing with these gurus. I'm sure many of you have seen me deal with it. I decided I'd rather spend time with my kids than focus my time on dealing with relentless attacks from self-proclaimed gurus.

They just go around telling people they are clueless, but the minute you call them out and platform their bad predictions, they have no courage to deal with it. 

Instead, they delete it all, block me, and they hope everyone forgets. 

I hope this guy chooses to unblock me and can communicate in better ways. Just because his views on rates were wrong in the past does not mean it is never worthwhile to listen to his view on rates in the future. In fact, it's the people who get things wrong who learn the hard way, who often can improve and learn from their mistakes.

I've made mistakes in the past and publicly announce when I'm wrong. 

Ego is what gets in the way of people becoming better investors.
